---
title: "Finding unobserved groups"
---

Imagine removing the vowel labels from a table of acoustic measurements and plotting the first two formants. Would the tokens still fall into recurring groups? And if they did, what—if anything—would license us to call those groups vowel categories?

We will ask these questions using Peterson and Barney's [vowel-production study](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1906875), distributed as [`phonTools::pb52`](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/phonTools/html/pb52.html) in package version 0.2-2.2. Each row represents one recorded /hVd/ vowel token. Speakers, elicitation words, and intended vowels repeat across rows, though we withhold the observed intended-vowel labels from the procedures that form the groups.

In the [Gaussian mixture](gaussian-mixtures.qmd), the component assignment is a **latent variable**: a [random variable](../random-variables-and-distributions/why-random-variables.qmd) whose realized value is not recorded in the table. The intended-vowel label is observed experimental metadata, which we use only after fitting to help interpret the unobserved component assignments. We begin by deciding how to represent a token and measure acoustic distance, then use [K-means](k-means.qmd) and Gaussian mixtures to find structure in that representation. Finally, we compare the fitted groups with intended-vowel labels and with measurements from held-out speakers.

```{r}
#| label: latent-index-data

stopifnot(as.character(packageVersion("phonTools")) == "0.2.2.2")
data("pb52", package = "phonTools")

speaker_id <- with(
  pb52,
  interaction(type, sex, speaker, drop = TRUE)
)

latent_inventory <- data.frame(
  unit = c(
    "vowel-token rows",
    "speakers",
    "tokens per speaker",
    "intended vowels"
  ),
  count = c(
    nrow(pb52),
    length(unique(speaker_id)),
    unique(as.integer(table(speaker_id))),
    length(unique(pb52$vowel))
  )
)

stopifnot(nrow(latent_inventory) == 4L)
latent_inventory
```

One source row can be read before any clustering notation is introduced:

```{r}
index_example <- pb52[1, c(
  "type", "sex", "speaker", "vowel", "repetition", "f1", "f2"
)]
index_example$elicitation_word <- "heed"
index_example
```

This row is the first repetition of *heed* by speaker 1 in the men's group. F1 and
F2 are the first two vocal-tract resonances, measured in hertz in a steady-state
part of the vowel. The [Peterson-Barney measurement
dossier](representing-objects.qmd#loading-and-checking-the-production-table)
decodes all ten elicitation labels, all source codes, and the dependence created
by two repetitions from each speaker.

The fitting representation contains F1 and F2 but not the elicitation word or intended-vowel label. The linguistic question is whether recurring regions appear in this acoustic representation and, if so, how they relate to categories supplied by the experimental design.

A group is unobserved only in the sense that no group label is supplied to the fitting procedure. A fitted cluster or mixture component is not automatically a phoneme, a vowel category, or a speaker type. That interpretation requires a separate comparison with linguistic metadata or held-out measurements.

## Hard clustering

The analysis begins by [representing each object](representing-objects.qmd) as a row of measurements. [Distance and scaling](distance-and-scaling.qmd) then determine which token pairs count as similar. Because F1 and F2 have different empirical spreads, the transformation affects the geometry supplied to the clustering algorithm.

[K-means](k-means.qmd) assigns each token to one cluster and represents each cluster by a centroid. The assignment and centroid updates minimize [within-cluster loss](within-cluster-loss.qmd). [Silhouette widths](silhouette-scores.qmd) compare each token's distance to its assigned cluster with its distance to the nearest alternative. [Validation without outcome labels](unsupervised-validation.qmd) then asks how centroids estimated from other speakers reconstruct a complete unseen-speaker panel.

## Finite mixture models

A [**finite mixture model**](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/finite-mixtures.html) represents a distribution as a weighted combination of component distributions. A [Gaussian mixture](gaussian-mixtures.qmd) uses Gaussian components for the acoustic measurements. [Posterior membership probabilities](posterior-membership.qmd) are conditional probabilities for the latent component after an acoustic vector is observed, and [expectation--maximization](expectation-maximization.qmd) alternates between updating these responsibilities and the component parameters.

A [likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) is the joint density of the observed data viewed as a function of model parameters. [Choosing a mixture with BIC](choosing-a-mixture.qmd) compares fitted likelihoods after accounting for parameter count. BIC still treats token rows as likelihood contributions, so the repeated-speaker structure remains a limitation rather than disappearing into the criterion. [Held-out mixture validation](validating-a-mixture.qmd) then evaluates fitted density for speakers absent during fitting and uses intended vowels only for a separate post-fit alignment check.

| Question | Hard clustering | Gaussian mixture |
|---|---|---|
| Assignment | One nearest centroid per token | A probability vector over components |
| Fitted target | Within-cluster squared distance | Token-level mixture likelihood |
| Overlap | Discarded by the hard assignment | Retained through responsibilities |
| Validation | Held-out distance to a training centroid | Held-out negative log density |

The table distinguishes algorithms before either result is given a linguistic
name. Neither objective makes a fitted group a phoneme.

## Module recap

1. The represented object and its scale determine which acoustic relations an
   algorithm can use.
2. K-means summarizes hard nearest-centroid geometry; a mixture supplies a
   probability model for overlap.
3. Validation must hold out speakers while naming the complete-panel information
   available at prediction time.

The probability calculations rely on [random variables and
distributions](../random-variables-and-distributions/index.qmd), while both
validation analyses reuse the [training--test separation
rule](../model-criticism-and-prediction/training-and-test-data.qmd#the-separation-rule).
Begin with the [measurement dossier](representing-objects.qmd#loading-and-checking-the-production-table).
